findings.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py:503 — P2 advisory, confidence 75: `!= integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` rejects the original installer after a GitHub username change when reconnecting an existing unlinked installation because OAuth supplies the current login while metadata retains the installation-time login; the strongest rebuttal is that installation normally completes immediately, but reconnecting an older installation still follows this branch and rejects the same account, so identity comparison must use the stable user ID ([GitHub username-change documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/how-tos/account-management/changing-your-username)).

src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py:503 — [P1, confidence 100] `!= integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` raises KeyError when an active integration created by `build_integration` without optional sender metadata is reattached after its OrganizationIntegration is removed, aborting setup with a server error instead of rendering the invalid-installation response.

src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py:423 — [P2, confidence 75] `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` executes outside the exception handler and `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` has no handler either, so a propagated connection or HTTP exception from either new OAuth request aborts the setup callback without rendering the failure dialog or notifying its opener.

src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py:482 — [P1, confidence 100] `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` bypasses the new installer-identity check when an installation webhook has not created its local Integration row, allowing an attacker authenticated with their own GitHub account to supply another valid installation_id and attach that installation to their Sentry organization because build_integration fetches it with app credentials without checking the authenticated user.

tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py:392 — P2 confidence 75: `{"code": "12345678901234567890", "state": "ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"}` sends a different state from the successful flows and the replacement `assert b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content` accepts the OAuth state-rejection response before the stubbed installation 404 is reached, so `test_installation_not_found` no longer detects regressions in the missing-installation behavior it claims to verify.

tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py:417 — Advisory P2 confidence 100: `webhook_event["sender"]["login"] = "attacker"` supplies the only webhook-created installation exercised by the changed tests and tests only rejection, so replacing the new sender comparison with unconditional rejection leaves those tests satisfied while blocking legitimate installers; the strongest rebuttal is that `test_basic_flow` asserts successful installation, but that flow creates no existing integration and exits through `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` before the new comparison.

tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py:120 — Advisory P2 confidence 100: `body=f"access_token={access_token}"` and `responses.add(responses.GET, self.base_url + "/user", json={"login": "octocat"})` force every exercised OAuth exchange onto successful token and identity responses, leaving the newly added decoding failure, missing-access-token and missing-login branches untested and allowing regressions in failure reporting to reach users with rejected GitHub authorizations; the strongest rebuttal is that the mismatch and invalid-state tests assert the failure template, but neither drives these token or identity failure branches.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py:503 — P2 advisory, confidence 75: `!= integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` rejects the original installer after a GitHub username change when reconnecting an existing unlinked installation because OAuth supplies the current login while metadata retains the installation-time login; the strongest rebuttal is that installation normally completes immediately, but reconnecting an older installation still follows this branch and rejects the same account, so identity comparison must use the stable user ID ([GitHub username-change documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/how-tos/account-management/changing-your-username)).

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows at line 503 that the code compares `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` (which comes from `authenticated_user_info["login"]` at line 441) against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. Both use the GitHub username ('login' field) for comparison. GitHub allows users to change their username, and the metadata stores the username at installation time while OAuth returns the current username. If a user changes their GitHub username between installation and reconnection, this comparison would fail even for the legitimate installer. The finding correctly identifies that using the stable user ID instead of the mutable login would be more robust.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py:423 — [P2, confidence 75] `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` executes outside the exception handler and `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` has no handler either, so a propagated connection or HTTP exception from either new OAuth request aborts the setup callback without rendering the failure dialog or notifying its opener.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that `safe_urlopen` at line 423 and `get_user_info` at line 431 are called without exception handling. Looking at the diff, the try/except block only wraps `safe_urlread(req).decode('utf-8')` and `dict(parse_qsl(body))`, not the `safe_urlopen` call itself. If `safe_urlopen` raises a network exception (timeout, connection error, etc.), or if `get_user_info` fails with an HTTP/network error, the exception would propagate up and abort the setup callback without rendering the error dialog. This is a real defect in the error handling logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py:482 — [P1, confidence 100] `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` bypasses the new installer-identity check when an installation webhook has not created its local Integration row, allowing an attacker authenticated with their own GitHub account to supply another valid installation_id and attach that installation to their Sentry organization because build_integration fetches it with app credentials without checking the authenticated user.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a security bypass. Looking at the diff, when `Integration.DoesNotExist` is caught at line 482, the code calls `pipeline.next_step()` without performing the installer-identity check that happens later (lines 493-499). This means if the webhook hasn't created the Integration row yet, an attacker who authenticates with their own GitHub account could supply someone else's valid installation_id. The subsequent `build_integration` in the pipeline would fetch the installation using app credentials (not user credentials), allowing the attacker to claim an installation they didn't create. The new OAuth flow validates the authenticated user matches `integration.metadata['sender']['login']`, but this check is completely bypassed when the Integration doesn't exist yet.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py:392 — P2 confidence 75: `{"code": "12345678901234567890", "state": "ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"}` sends a different state from the successful flows and the replacement `assert b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content` accepts the OAuth state-rejection response before the stubbed installation 404 is reached, so `test_installation_not_found` no longer detects regressions in the missing-installation behavior it claims to verify.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that test_installation_not_found uses state 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05' while successful flows use '9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3'. Looking at OAuthLoginView.dispatch(), when request.GET.get('state') != pipeline.signature, it returns error() with 'Invalid installation request.' message. Since the test uses a mismatched state, it will fail at the OAuth state validation before ever reaching the installation lookup logic. The test assertion changed from checking 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' to 'Invalid installation request.' - confirming the test now validates OAuth state rejection rather than the missing installation scenario it claims to test.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py:417 — Advisory P2 confidence 100: `webhook_event["sender"]["login"] = "attacker"` supplies the only webhook-created installation exercised by the changed tests and tests only rejection, so replacing the new sender comparison with unconditional rejection leaves those tests satisfied while blocking legitimate installers; the strongest rebuttal is that `test_basic_flow` asserts successful installation, but that flow creates no existing integration and exits through `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` before the new comparison.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test coverage gap. Looking at the diff, the new sender comparison check at lines 499-503 validates that `pipeline.fetch_state('github_authenticated_user') != integration.metadata['sender']['login']`. The test `test_github_user_mismatch` only tests the rejection case (when users don't match). The `test_basic_flow` (via `assert_setup_flow`) does reach the OAuth flow but creates a new installation that doesn't exist yet, so it exits via `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` before reaching the sender comparison. This means there's no test that verifies the happy path where an existing integration's sender matches the authenticated user. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added security logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py:120 — Advisory P2 confidence 100: `body=f"access_token={access_token}"` and `responses.add(responses.GET, self.base_url + "/user", json={"login": "octocat"})` force every exercised OAuth exchange onto successful token and identity responses, leaving the newly added decoding failure, missing-access-token and missing-login branches untested and allowing regressions in failure reporting to reach users with rejected GitHub authorizations; the strongest rebuttal is that the mismatch and invalid-state tests assert the failure template, but neither drives these token or identity failure branches.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new OAuth flow in OAuthLoginView has multiple error branches (exception during token parsing at lines 430-431, missing 'access_token' at lines 433-434, missing 'login' at lines 437-438) that are not covered by the test changes. The test stubs at lines 116-122 always return successful responses, and while there are tests for user mismatch and invalid state, none of the tests exercise the token exchange failure paths or identity lookup failures. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added nontrivial error handling logic.
